From CVR numbers to accounting data

Source: vignettes/cvrr.Rmd
cvrr.Rmd

The cvr_* functions fetch published annual reports from Erhvervsstyrelsens distribution service, and read_xbrl() turns the machine-readable ones into data. The service is official, free, and built for system-to-system access, and annual reports are public documents by law. Using it is legitimate. Using it well is a matter of a few habits, and this article is as much about those as about the function calls.

The pipeline

Four functions, one step each: build the query, send it, extract the hits, download the documents.

cvr_query(
  cvr          = c("12345678", "87654321"),
  enddate_from = "2024-01-01",
  enddate_to   = "2024-12-31"
) |>
  cvr_search(contact = "you@example.com") |>
  cvr_hits() |>
  cvr_download("data/pdf")
  • cvr_query() builds the Elasticsearch query (pure, no network). Matches by CVR number (max 1000 per query) and accounting-period end date.
  • cvr_search() posts the query and returns the parsed response.
  • cvr_hits() flattens the response into a tibble with one row per document (cvrnummer, dokumenturl, …).
  • cvr_download() downloads the documents and returns the hits tibble with a path and a downloaded column, so every file can be traced back to the row it came from.

Everything before cvr_search() is local; that line is the first real API call.

CVR numbers from a spreadsheet or another register often carry a DK prefix, spaces or dashes, and cvr_query() accepts only 8 digits. clean_cvr() brings them to that form without inventing digits, so a seven-digit number stays visibly wrong:

clean_cvr(c("DK12345678", "12 34 56 78", "1234567"))
#> [1] "12345678" "12345678" "1234567"

Greenlandic companies

Greenland’s own business register (GER) was folded into CVR on 3 January 2018. Greenlandic companies therefore have ordinary 8-digit CVR numbers, appear in the same distribution service, and file under the same Danish GAAP taxonomy — nothing in this package treats them differently. The one consequence to plan for is the start date: filings from before 2018 are not reachable here under a CVR number.

Identify yourself

The contact argument is mandatory and is sent as the User-Agent header. Erhvervsstyrelsen asks requests to identify the sender, so use a real email address you can be reached at. The function refuses to run with an empty contact, but it cannot check that the address is honest; that part is yours.

Be polite about volume

Each hit is one published annual report, and its dokumenter array typically holds several files (PDF, XML/XBRL, sometimes XHTML), so expect roughly 3-5 document rows per company per year in the hits tibble.

The query selects companies and periods. Selecting which documents to download is done in R, between cvr_hits() and cvr_download():

hits <- hits[hits$dokumentmimetype == "application/pdf", ]

The arithmetic matters: 1000 companies for one year is ~1000 hits but 3000-5000 documents, which at the default sleep = 3 is 2.5-4 hours of downloading. Filtering to one mimetype first cuts it to ~1000 files (under an hour). Always look at the hits tibble before you call cvr_download(); it tells you exactly what you are about to fetch.

cvr_download() enforces a delay of at least 1 second between requests (default 3). By default it refuses to start if any of the files it would write already exist. A run of that size will sometimes be interrupted, so to carry on where it stopped:

files <- cvr_download(hits, "data/pdf", overwrite = "skip")
files[!files$downloaded, ]      # what still needs another attempt

Files are named by CVR number alone, which means a company’s filings for different years are told apart only by a _2, _3 suffix in whatever order the API returned them. When you are pulling several years, name them by period instead:

cvr_download(hits, "data/xml", name_by = c("cvrnummer", "slutdato"))

Complete results: scroll

A single response holds at most query$size hits (default 2999). cvr_search() warns if the response is full, since the result may then be truncated. For large pulls (many companies across many years), use the scroll API to fetch every matching hit in batches:

response <- cvr_query(many_cvrs, "2015-01-01", "2024-12-31") |>
  cvr_search(contact = "you@example.com", scroll = TRUE)

scroll affects the completeness of the search result only. It does not reduce the number of documents you download afterwards. A scroll of a large panel makes hundreds of requests, so transient failures are retried with a backoff rather than discarding the whole pull.

Test small first

Before a big pull, run the pipeline on a handful of companies and a narrow date range, inspect the hits tibble, and only then scale up. If you want to see the scroll mechanics work without load, force small batches: scroll = 2 on a query with a few hits walks through the whole flow in a couple of requests.

Working with the XBRL files

The PDF is the human-readable version of the annual report. For data work, the XML file next to it is usually the better download: it is XBRL, the machine-readable filing, and read_xbrl() parses it into a tidy tibble with one row per reported fact.

hits_xml <- hits[hits$dokumentmimetype == "application/xml", ]
cvr_download(hits_xml, "materiale/xbrl")

x <- read_xbrl("materiale/xbrl")

That is the whole read. read_xbrl() takes a directory, a vector of paths or a single file; it binds the filings into one table, resolves the taxonomy on the way in, and carries each filing’s own identity — file, cvr, period_start, period_end — on every row.

Binding filings by hand is the part worth not doing yourself: each contributes only the dimension columns it actually uses, so do.call(rbind, ...) fails and rbindlist(fill = TRUE) is needed.

Four things to know about the result:

  • value is the figure, fact is the text. The conversion happens once, on the way in. A fact the filer declared numeric that will not parse is reported rather than silently dropped to NA.
  • A filing carries several accounting years. period is the date a fact belongs to and period_end is the year the filing is about, so x$period == x$period_end is the closing column.
  • prefix and namespace identify the element. A Danish filing binds six or more namespaces at once, and the taxonomy is keyed by the namespace plus the local name, not by elementid alone.
  • dimensions and explicit_member carry the breakdowns, including ConsolidatedSoloDimension. Roughly a fifth of the contexts in a real filing carry two dimensions, and consolidated figures sit next to the parent company’s own. is_line marks the figures that are the statement line itself rather than a breakdown of it.

The tables

xbrl_accounts() divides the facts into what an analysis reads.

a <- xbrl_accounts(x)

a$company           # who the company is
a$location          # where it is
a$audit             # who audited it, who filed it, with what tool
a$checks            # whether any of it adds up
a$income_statement  # lines, in statement order
a$balance           # lines, with the ones the filer left out derived
a$cash_flow         # the cash flow statement, as reported
a$movements         # the fixed asset note, movement by movement
a$prose             # what management wrote

Every table opens with the same key — cvr, name, period_start, period_end — so moving between them needs no looking, and every table ends with file, so a figure can be traced back to the document it came from. The three statements carry reconciled on every row, so filtering to the lines that add up needs no join; a$checks gathers the per-filing verdicts, and they are several columns rather than one because a filing can have a balance sheet that closes and an income statement that does not.

a$movements is the fixed asset schedule as it is printed: one row per movement, per asset class, per filing, with layer naming the block (cost, depreciation, revaluation, carrying), item the row within it (opening, additions, disposals, transfers, charge, reversals, closing) and label the two of them as a note prints the line — “Kostpris primo”, “Tilgang”, “Årets af- og nedskrivninger”. The labels are the package’s own: opening and closing are the same taxonomy element at two dates, so the taxonomy’s label names both and distinguishes neither.

The signs are solved and applied. A Danish filing writes a disposal positive about as often as negative, so value carries the sign that makes the block roll forward — a disposal is negative in it whatever the filer wrote — and tagged keeps the filer’s own number beside it. sign_source says where the sign came from: balance for a stated opening or closing amount, solved where the block’s arithmetic settled it, and convention where nothing could be solved and the direction was taken from what the row is.

# what these companies invested in tangible assets, per year
add <- a$movements[a$movements$category == "tangible" &
                     a$movements$item == "additions", ]
tapply(add$value, format(add$period_end, "%Y"), sum)

The three functions behind it — xbrl_company(), xbrl_lines() and xbrl_movements() — can be called on their own when only one table is wanted, and xbrl_lines() reaches the statements xbrl_accounts() does not return:

xbrl_lines(x, "equity")

Validate once

Everything from here on needs the same work done first: the tagging put right, the statements checked and solved. xbrl_validate() does it once and attaches it to the facts, so the screen, the panel and every report read it instead of repeating it:

v <- xbrl_validate(x)

v is still the facts, one row per fact. A panel is a view cut from them, and it would drop the notes, the dimensions and where each figure came from. Keep v and cut what is needed. A subset of whole filings keeps the work, and a filing whose figures have changed since is done again rather than read from stale work.

A panel to analyse

The tables above are the filings as they are presented. For analysis the same figures are wanted as variables: one row per company and year. xbrl_panel() builds that from the statements, after the tagging has been put right:

p <- xbrl_panel(v)
p[c("cvr", "period_end", "gross_profit", "operating_profit", "equity",
    "balance_reconciled")]

Costs are positive amounts, a loss is negative, and tax is the result before tax less the result after it, so its sign is right whatever the filer wrote. net_financials is found the same way and is the complete figure; finance_income and finance_expenses are only the lines with those names. A figure the filing does not report stays NA. Each row carries the company’s class, form, assurance and group, and three verdicts on whether its statements add up. Excluding a row on them is left to the analysis.

Two functions read the panel. xbrl_ratios() adds the published ratios, the change from the previous annual report, and the median and percentile among comparable companies. xbrl_robustness() adds the signs of vulnerability from Danmarks Nationalbank’s bankruptcy model, with capital lost and going concern added, and two buffers:

r <- xbrl_robustness(p)
attr(r, "validation")    # each factor against the companies that stopped filing

Comparable means the same accounting class unless told otherwise. A branch of industry is better and is not in a filing; join it on cvr and pass its column as group.

A report

The whole chain ends in a page. xbrl_report() writes one HTML file, and which report it is follows from the filings given: one company in one year, one company over time, many companies in one year, or many over several:

xbrl_report(v, "company.html", cvr = "12345678", peers = p)
xbrl_report(v, "all.html")

It opens with what matters most, as sentences. Each sentence is a rule with a threshold: the auditor’s opinion, a loss for the second year running, an equity ratio that fell five points or more, cash that covers less than a month’s wages, a place in the bottom tenth among peers. The tables follow. xbrl_report_data() returns the same content as data, so a report of one’s own can use it.

Signs

XBRL amounts often arrive without a meaningful sign: costs can be reported as positive numbers, and the convention varies between preparers. find_signs() recovers them, because the income statement has to reconcile — it searches for the +1/-1 assignment that makes the line items sum to the reported total.

The reconciliation is per company and per year, so say so with by. Without it, every company’s ProfitLoss row lands in the same group and nothing reconciles:

income <- x[x$elementid %in% c(
  "Revenue", "ExternalExpenses", "EmployeeBenefitsExpense",
  "TaxExpense", "ProfitLoss"
), ]

signs <- find_signs(income, elementid, value,
                    total_label = "ProfitLoss",
                    by = c(cvr, period_end))

table(signs$status)

Nothing is dropped. Every input row comes back with a status:

  • unique — one assignment reaches the total.
  • ambiguous — several do, but items every candidate agreed on are still filled in, flagged certain = TRUE.
  • unsolved — none did, usually because the set of line items is incomplete.
  • no_total / duplicate_total — the group had no ProfitLoss row, or more than one.

Read unique as “only one combination reaches the total”, not as “this combination is right”. If the true assignment was excluded, a coincidental one can fit alone. The element names depend on the taxonomy the company filed under, so start by looking at the elementid values in your own data before hardcoding a selection.

The taxonomy

Everything above works on the numbers alone. The names, the statement each figure belongs to, and its debit/credit convention live in the taxonomy the filing points at with a single link:schemaRef — and that URI is an identifier, not a download address. Get the package from Erhvervsstyrelsen, once per year of taxonomy, and open it:

tax <- read_taxonomy("XBRL20241001.zip")
x   <- read_xbrl("materiale/xbrl", taxonomy = tax)

bs <- x[x$statement == "BalanceSheetAccountForm" & x$is_line, ]
bs[order(bs$code), c("code", "label", "balance", "basis", "value")]

The code is the taxonomy’s own numbering, so 400.00.020.010.020 is “Assets, non-current, property plant and equipment” and sorts into statement order by itself. It is stable across companies and years.

Pass a list of taxonomies when the filings span versions — and they will. The version a filing declares follows when it was prepared, so a single accounting year routinely spans several.

Parent company or group

basis says which, and basis_source says how it was decided. Group figures are tagged with a member of ConsolidatedSoloDimension; parent-company figures are not tagged at all. Reading that absence as “parent” is only legitimate because the taxonomy declares a default member for the dimension, which read_taxonomy() reads rather than assumes. Never add the two together.

Reconciling 

bs <- x[x$statement %in% c("BalanceSheetAccountForm", "BalanceSheetReportForm") &
          x$basis == "parent", ]
checks <- check_statement(bs)
table(checks$verdict)
#>              complete            conflicting             duplicates
#>                 33252                     25                    217
#>           sides agree          two groupings  unspecified remainder
#>                  4304                   4210                    195

Each subtotal is compared with the nearest reported lines below it — nearest, because a filer may report a figure while leaving its intermediate parent empty. Three outcomes matter:

  • complete — the reported detail exhausts the subtotal and can be used as it stands. This is the normal result: an unreported line means “not applicable”, not “unknown”.
  • two groupings — the same figures under two groupings. A Danish balance sheet lists debt both by counterparty and by maturity, so the children sum to a multiple of the subtotal. Not an error.
  • unspecified remainder — real detail the filing did not break down.
  • sides differ — the statement’s debit and credit sides do not meet. It does not appear above because every one of the 4,304 balance sheets closes; on an income statement the sides are not meant to meet at all, since it is a cascade, which is what check_cascade() walks.

The income statement is not checked this way, because its lines carry signs. That is what find_signs() is for, and the two are independent: one reads a published file, the other only adds up the numbers in front of it.

Screening a pile of filings

Each check answers one question about one statement. xbrl_screen() asks all of them of every filing and returns the answers worth reading, one row per finding, most serious and largest first:

s <- xbrl_screen(x)
s[c("cvr", "name", "period_end", "check", "finding", "share", "severity")]

share is the amount against the filing’s total assets, and a finding under 1% of them moves down a level, so the list is ordered by what matters rather than by kroner.

The tagging is put right first. A filing now and then tags a line in thousands where it is in kroner, most often in its comparative column, and screened as it stands that outranks every real finding. Over the 4,304 filings of 2020-2024 it was 41 of the 54 serious findings. xbrl_screen() therefore runs xbrl_standardise() before it looks. A comparative is corrected where the filing disagrees with itself: its own year and the earlier filing agree, and the comparative is a thousand off. A cash flow sign is reversed where its activity adds up only that way. A contrary sign the activity adds up with stays, because then it means something. Greenland Airports’ sale of a company reported negative is one of those. Everything else is left as tagged and listed in attr(s, "technical"), apart from the findings:

attr(s, "technical")    # 147 units and 17 signs corrected, 49 undecided

What is left is the accounts and what the auditor said about them. 618 filings have a finding. The serious ones are 81 auditor’s opinions that are qualified, adverse or missing, and 13 cash flow statements that do not add up. Each row carries the filing’s class, legal form, level of assurance and whether it belongs to a group, so a finding can be set beside its kind. A unit error shows only when a filing is set beside the one before it, because everything inside a single filing is consistent, so pass several years.

The cash flow statement, against the rest

A cash flow statement can be wrong in a way its own arithmetic never shows. Move an amount from one activity to another and every total still adds up. That is what happened in Greenland Airports’ 2025 group accounts (CVR 12859724). A state grant of DKK 400 million was reported as “Optagelse af langfristet gæld”, and 364 million of it was taken to income and then put under investing as an outflow, tagged in the XBRL as SaleOfOtherCompany. check_cashflow() holds the statement against the balance sheet, the income statement and the fixed asset note:

x  <- read_xbrl("gai")   # the group's filings, from cvr_download()
cf <- check_cashflow(x)
cf[cf$check %in% c("activities", "rollforward", "cash vs balance",
                   "debt vs balance"),
   c("check", "reported", "expected", "residual", "offset_by", "verdict")]
#>   check              reported    expected   residual offset_by                     verdict
#>   activities       -298706000  -298706000          0 <NA>                          agrees
#>   rollforward        65251000    65251000          0 <NA>                          agrees
#>   cash vs balance    65251000    65251000          0 <NA>                          agrees
#>   debt vs balance  1157390000   793390000  364000000 investing: SaleOfOtherCompany borrowed more than owed

Every internal check passes. The borrowing does not appear in the balance sheet, and offset_by names the line in investing that takes the same amount back out. A reclassification has to leave a gap in two places, equal and opposite, and that pair is what separates it from the ordinary reasons debt and cash part company. Across the 328 Danish filings in the corpus that tag a cash flow statement, that pairing with borrowing the balance sheet does not owe turns up nowhere.

Movements through the year

check_statement() compares instants with instants and check_cascade() durations with durations. Neither touches the identity that binds them, and it is the one an accounts statistic most needs, because the movements are where a company states what it invested:

schedules <- c("StatementOfChangesInEquityLongVersion", "DisclosureOfEquity",
               "DisclosureOfAssets")
moves <- check_movement(x, statement = schedules)
moves[c("group", "member", "opening", "closing", "status")]

Scoping matters here. A roll-forward is recognised by its shape — one balance at both ends of the year, movements beside it — and two other kinds of group have that shape without the meaning. A five-year summary sets assets, equity and provisions at two dates each, so nothing says which of them the profit in the same group explains; those are skipped because they hold more than one balance. The related-party note quotes equity and profit alone, which is exactly the shape of an equity statement, and no structural rule can tell them apart. Naming the statements is what separates them.

Where a filer tags the movements only per class and leaves the total column untagged, the classes are summed and movements says so — the identity then tests that sum as well.

Handing it to a statistic

The package stops at the filing’s own lines. Which element is turnover, which is staff costs, and what to do when a filing gives neither, are decisions that belong to the statistic’s variable definitions and change when those change. cvrr’s job is to hand over the lines with their taxonomy label, their code and their sign convention, and to be honest about which of them are derived.

Two things about the Danish and Greenlandic corpus are worth knowing before picking elements, because neither is visible in a spot check.

A top line is not necessarily turnover. A company in accounting class B may present a gross figure instead of turnover, and most do: 82% of the 4,304 filings carry GrossProfitLoss and 19% GrossResult, against 14% that carry Revenue at all. Gross profit is turnover net of cost of sales, so treating the two as one column produces a turnover series that is quietly too small for four filings in five — and nothing downstream can tell, because a number is a number.

inc <- a$income_statement
table(inc$elementid[inc$elementid %in% c("Revenue", "GrossProfitLoss")])

Staff costs come split or whole. Of the 2,873 filings that report them at all, 1,650 give wages, pension or social security separately and 1,334 give only EmployeeBenefitsExpense. Adding that total into a wages column overstates wages by the pension and social security it contains.

And a limit that is in the source rather than in the parsing: 59 of the 82 variables Danmarks Statistik’s Regnskabsstatistik asks for live in the taxonomy’s own InformationForStatisticsDenmark section — turnover split into own production and goods for resale, rent excluding heating, additions to buildings separately from land — and not one filing of 4,304 fills in any of it.

The balance sheet, repaired

xbrl_lines(x, "balance") returns the balance sheet as lines, in statement order, with the ones the filer left out solved from the identities and marked as solved:

b <- xbrl_lines(x, "balance")
b[b$source != "reported", c("elementid", "value", "source")]

The repair matters more than it sounds. Half the filings never state long-term debt — not because it is secret, but because there is none, or because the total and the short-term part already say what it is. Reading that as “unknown” throws away half the population:

                                    reported   after solving
long-term debt                          49%            97%
provisions                              55%            98%
non-current assets                      85%            99%
current assets                          94%           100%

The hierarchy alone cannot do this. LiabilitiesOtherThanProvisions has 33 children in the taxonomy, because the same debts are presented twice — by kind, and by term — so summing the reported ones counts every krone twice. Five named identities are partitions rather than presentations, and each is solved for its single unknown. Each was checked first: all five hold to within a krone for 99–100% of the filings that state every term.

How right is a solved figure? It was held out and checked: on 400 filings that do state long-term debt, the figure was hidden and solved for. It came back exactly right for 397 and within a tenth of a percent for 398.

Nothing derived is called reported. About two thousand of the recovered long-term figures are nought, which is a value and not a gap — but it is a value the filing did not write down, and source says so.

The company behind the figures

Accounts on their own are not a statistic. xbrl_company() reads the background out of the same filing — identity, period, accounting class, auditor, employees, and the management’s own description of what the company does and how the year went:

xbrl_company(x)

xbrl_accounts() divides that row into four: company for who this is, location for where, audit for how the report came to be, and prose for what management wrote. It is 40 columns as one row, and the prose fields run to hundreds of characters.

Every filing states its CVR number, name, accounting class, the type of auditor’s assistance, its period and the date of the general meeting. Most state the address (82%), what the company does (79%), the audit firm and its CVR number (78%), how the year went (76%) and the average number of employees (74%). 99% say something about either their activity or their year.

reporting_class keeps the filing’s own words — it is where “mikrovirksomhed” is visible — and class carries just the letter, which matters because 13 filings write the class in English and grouping on the verbatim field would quietly make two populations out of one.

Two things are worth knowing before relying on it.

The industry is not in the filing. The taxonomy has a place for it and not one filing of 4,304 uses it. A company’s industry has to come from the register, where it arrives as a code and a label in a single field. No empty column is returned for it here, because an always-NA column reads as “unknown” rather than “never asked for”.

Nor is the legal form – the taxonomy has no element for it at all. But company law puts it in the name, so form is read from there: 99.6% of 4,304 filings carry a recognisable one. That is a reading of a string the law decides the contents of, not a guess; where it matters, the register is the authority.

The activity description is not under the name you would guess. DisclosureOfMainActivitiesAndAccountingAndFinancialMatters sounds right and is used by 7% of filings; DescriptionOfPrimaryActivitiesOfEntity is used by 72%. Both are read, and activity_source says which one answered. development works the same way, falling back from the tagged description of the year to the management’s review as a whole.

Not everything is in kroner

currency is what the filing states its amounts in, and it is worth checking before anything is added up. Of 4,304 filings, 4,293 are kroner — and eight are not: six report in Canadian dollars and two in US dollars, all of them Greenlandic companies with foreign owners. Three more are US dollars throughout with a single stray nil fact tagged DKK, and come back as "DKK+USD" so that filtering on "DKK" does not quietly let them in.

Nothing is converted. Every table that hands out amounts carries the column, so the currency travels with the figure:

kroner <- a$balance[a$balance$currency == "DKK", ]
tapply(kroner$value[kroner$elementid == "Assets"],
       format(kroner$period_end[kroner$elementid == "Assets"], "%Y"), sum)

Eight filings in four thousand is the kind of thing that survives every spot check and then puts Canadian dollars into a krone total.

Persons

A filing names people: the auditor, the executive board, the chairman of the general meeting. Those are personal data and an accounts statistic does not need them — the audit firm and its CVR number answer “who audited this” without naming anyone — so they are left out unless asked for:

xbrl_company(x, persons = TRUE)[c("auditor_name", "executive_board")]

Use it where there is a reason, and remember the result then carries names that should not be redistributed casually.

The legal frame

Annual reports are public by law, and the distribution service is the channel Erhvervsstyrelsen provides for exactly this kind of retrieval. Usage falls under the general terms for Danish open public data. The one substantive restriction to know about is reklamebeskyttelse (CVR-lovens paragraf 19): data on protected companies must not be used for direct marketing. For statistical and analytical use of financial statements, that restriction is irrelevant, but if your use case ever drifts toward contacting the companies, check it.
